name: Omar Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Omar, 43, with a master’s in music. I lead percussion for a regional concert hall, record short drum parts for local adverts and teach six advanced pupils. I am one of the stronger players here, but leading means knowing when another player needs room. I enjoy the silence after a good final beat; I dislike an advert client reusing a recording without asking the people who played it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps the household running around the music?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works regular hours as a school administrator, and our two children are school-age. We have a mortgage, about ten months of expenses saved, and my musician pay is higher than most local players’. There are plenty of similar jobs nearby, though a vacancy is not mine until an offer. I have never used an AI tool and keep my rehearsal notes on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the hall that a cleaner schedule is welcome if every rehearsal and concert still has a fee beside it. A percussion section needs eyes and ears, not just a printed count.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our mortgage is comfortable with ten months saved and my partner’s steady pay. I still check whether an advert buys one use of a drum part or a whole year of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the hall concerts and six pupils this season. This week I’d get the next paid dates and recording-reuse terms in writing, then save one fifth of each cleared advert fee after mortgage and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm in this mild version. A late cheque would be irritating, but it would not change our children’s school plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who sets the recording reuse price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advert studio sends a licence, meaning written permission for where a recording may be used. I ask the players to read it before we agree to another season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a tool for rehearsal notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used AI. I would let the office tidy the calendar, but I would still mark the notes I need on paper.

I would ask for written **recording reuse** terms before another season.
think: Our **ten-month reserve** and partner’s wage cover routine delays.
An unclear **advert licence** could still lose the players a fee.
do: Keep **hall concerts** and six pupils this season.
Confirm paid dates and **reuse terms**; save one fifth of cleared advert fees after bills.
feel: I feel **calm** because current paid work and savings cover a late cheque.
S0.quote: A percussion section needs eyes and ears, not just a printed count.
fieldNote: His **senior skill** and high pay support a strong cushion without guaranteeing every future recording.

steps.text: Keep paid hall concerts and six advanced pupils this season
Save fifth of each cleared advert fee after mortgage and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the hall that generated drum parts could remove paid studio hours before a robot can handle our instruments. I would ask the musicians’ union for a minimum recording fee and written reuse permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert recordings are about a quarter of my music pay. I expect some clients to choose generated parts, so a long cut would make our reserve grow more slowly even if concerts continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d bring my last season’s studio invoices to the union and ask it to seek a minimum fee and consent for each new use. In the first year, if advert orders fall, I’d stop hiring the extra rehearsal room on empty weekdays and keep the paid hall and pupil dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a real quarter of my income shrinking. Ten months saved lets us bargain carefully, but savings do not pay for a recording someone gets free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use an AI drummer to compete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI, and I would not upload a pupil’s playing or another player’s take without permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger player?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell them to ask what the session pays and how long a client may use it. A credit in small print is not a recording fee.

I would warn that **generated drum parts** may undercut paid studio work.
think: Advert recordings supply **one quarter** of my music pay.
A lasting cut would slow **reserve growth** despite paid concerts.

Stop **room hire** on empty weekdays if adverts fall; keep paid hall and pupils.
feel: I feel **anxious** about an expected cut to my own recording fees.
S1.quote: A credit in small print is not a recording fee.
fieldNote: His **advert income** is measurable and vulnerable despite high pay, strong savings and several nearby music employers.
He seeks **collective terms** and protects recordings from unconsented reuse.

steps.text: Ask union for minimum recording fees and reuse consent using studio invoices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the percussion section that thinking AGI by 2028 could make advert parts and plans cheaply, while capable robots for hands-on playing follow around 2031. I would ask the hall for written concert dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect studio recording fees to end quickly, and the hall might shorten a season if its clients cut budgets. Ten months saved buys a search, but it cannot make a lost quarter of income unimportant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I’d get the hall’s paid season and pupil hours in writing. In the first year after AGI arrives, if recording orders stop and concert dates shrink, I’d apply for an advertised arts-college percussion post only if it accepts my master’s and experience and written net pay after travel replaces the lost income with school pickup covered; I’d keep current hall and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the loss, but not lost for options. Several local music employers exist; I would need a real offer before giving up a good hall chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the college offer workable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare paid teaching and preparation hours with travel and a confirmed childcare rota. A title is not a wage when the preparation is unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend savings on an audition tour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would pay for one local audition if the vacancy and wage are stated. I would not spend ten months of reserve chasing unposted jobs.

I would ask for **written concert dates** before trusting the next season.
think: I expect **studio fees** to end and concert dates might shrink.
Our **ten-month reserve** buys search time, not replacement pay.
do: Keep **hall and pupils** until signed college offer; confirm paid dates before 2028.
Seek **college vacancy** if recordings stop and concerts shrink; require accepted master’s, paid preparation, written replacement pay after travel and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about lost recording income despite a cushion and local options.
S2.quote: A title is not a wage when the preparation is unpaid.
fieldNote: The **2028 recording loss** precedes robot percussion playing around 2031.
A college move requires **posted work**, accepted master’s, paid preparation, written replacement pay and covered pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the union that five years gives us time to price live work and test one small concert series. Thinking AGI can replace studio parts around 2031, while capable robot players follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An independent Saturday matinee could replace recording fees, but a full hall on a poster is not ticket money. I will not ask the other players to rehearse for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d ask an independent arts hall for a written fixed room fee and offer three Saturday percussion matinees only if sixty tickets are paid in advance and the receipts cover that fee, my preparation and performance, two other players’ rehearsal and performance, and confirmed childcare. In the first year after 2031 I’d repeat only if sixty paid tickets still cover those costs and the room contract and childcare hold, while keeping my paid hall concerts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about studio pay ending, though we have time and money to test one series carefully. Sixty people saying they might come is not sixty paid seats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay the other players before ticket sales?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not book them until the advance receipts cover their rehearsal and stage time. If only forty buy tickets, I would refund them and cancel before anyone loses pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would handle the instruments safely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the hall for a signed stage plan and make sure its staff approve where the drums stand. I would not put a large drum in an aisle used by children.

I would offer **paid matinees** only after ticket receipts cover the players.
think: Sixty **prepaid tickets** must cover the room and all three musicians.
A **poster crowd** is not the same as paid seats.
do: Request a **written fixed room fee**; start matinees only with sixty paid tickets covering room, all musicians' work and childcare.
Repeat the **matinees** after 2031 only if sixty tickets cover preparation/rehearsal, room contract and childcare.
Use a **signed stage plan** and staff approval before placing drums.
feel: I feel **anxious** about recording loss while testing a paid series.
S3.quote: Sixty people saying they might come is not sixty paid seats.
fieldNote: His **ticket gate** covers his preparation and performance plus two players’ rehearsal and stage fees.
A **signed stage plan** keeps large drums out of children’s aisles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my children that ten years is enough to learn an instrument and the value of a written session fee. Thinking AGI comes around 2036 and capable robot players around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still lead percussion, but studio recordings could be worth less by then. Our ten-month reserve and my partner’s pay make the next few years secure enough to plan without rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d keep hall concerts and six pupils and save one fifth of each cleared extra studio fee after mortgage and food, aiming for twelve months. Over the decade I’d offer matinees only if sixty advance paid tickets cover fixed room fee, my preparation and performance, two players’ rehearsal and performance, approved safe stage and childcare; in the first year after 2036 I’d repeat only while those paid conditions hold and seek an advertised college role if studio fees end, provided my master’s qualifies and written net pay after travel replaces losses with pickup covered, while keeping current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant recording pay, not the next mortgage instalment. A decade is useful only if the tickets and teaching hours turn into fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy more drums now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep our current kit maintained. I would save only after a studio fee clears and bills are paid, not from a promised recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the hall offers a free date but no stage plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put large drums beside a children’s exit. The hall must approve a safe plan before I sell the seats.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because recording fees could stop before the hall signs another season. Written concert dates, a posted college role with fair paid preparation and viable net pay, and actual ticket sales for a live series would help. Our reserve gives time to search, not a reason to play for free.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the percussion players before the curtain rises. The audience hears one final beat, but there were three paid rehearsals behind it.

headlineQuote: The audience hears one final beat, but there were three paid rehearsals behind it.
portrait: Omar is a **43-year-old percussion lead** with a music master’s, hall concerts, six pupils and advert recordings.
His **higher pay**, school-employed partner, mortgage and ten-month reserve support two school-age children.
He **never uses AI** and seeks union recording terms and paid live contracts.
Fast AGI threatens **studio fees** before robots play; he tests ticket-backed matinees and actual college posts.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** could end recording fees before the hall signs another season.
whatWouldHelp: Written **concert dates** and a posted college role paying preparation and viable net wages would help.
Sixty **paid tickets** covering all musicians would support a live series without unpaid rehearsals.
